solutions.AC9E3LA06-guided-1: the rain / fell; the children / were painting. While introduces the dependent rain clause; indoors is outside the verb group.
solutions.AC9E3LA06-guided-2: The bag of shells rests here: bag is the singular head of the whole subject The bag of shells. Sam and Lee carry it: the coordinated subject names two people.
solutions.AC9E3LA06-guided-3: We were by the gate. The small dog has a lead. We takes were in standard past usage; singular dog takes present has.
solutions.AC9E3LA06-tricky-1: Yes. Is relates the gate to its description open; a verb need not express visible action.
solutions.AC9E3LA06-tricky-2: No. Children, people and mice are plural without final -s; we and they also refer to plural subjects.
solutions.AC9E3LA06-tricky-3: Yes. A command such as Open the gate has an understood you as subject.
solutions.AC9E3LA07-guided-1: Pushed is doing: Jo applies force to move the gate. Called is saying here: Jo speaks Come in, plausibly so someone can hear; it does not prove anger or another motive.
solutions.AC9E3LA07-guided-2: Believed expresses thinking; loved expresses feeling.
solutions.AC9E3LA07-guided-3: Are in The toy boats are small and has in Each boat has a sail are relating verbs. Are moving is the whole doing verb group in the third clause; are alone is auxiliary there.
solutions.AC9E3LA07-tricky-1: Yes: in The boat is small, is is the complete verb group relating boat to a description.
solutions.AC9E3LA07-tricky-2: No. I think uses think alone, but I am thinking uses am thinking as the whole group. Other auxiliaries can also join, as in will think.
solutions.AC9E3LA07-tricky-3: No. Meaning in the full clause determines the label; has in She has a hat relates possession, but has in She has opened it helps another verb.
solutions.AC9E3LA08-guided-1: Feeds is the whole verb group in the first sentence, describing a repeated present habit supported by Every morning. Will feed is the whole verb group in the second, describing a future event supported by Tomorrow.
solutions.AC9E3LA08-guided-2: Yesterday Lee carried the tray. Lee took a cup. Tomorrow Lee will carry the tray. Carried changes y to i before -ed; took is irregular; carry is base form after will.
solutions.AC9E3LA08-guided-3: Yesterday Sam found a pot. He put soil in it. Tomorrow he will plant a seed. Replace puts with put for yesterday's second event; keep the deliberate shift to tomorrow and will plant.
solutions.AC9E3LA08-tricky-1: No. Present forms can describe habits/facts and, with context, future arrangements, as well as current events.
solutions.AC9E3LA08-tricky-2: No. Use will carry: will is followed by base carry, not carries.
solutions.AC9E3LA08-tricky-3: Use time phrases and surrounding clauses/context, including any auxiliaries. I put it there yesterday and I put it there every day use the same written put but different time contexts. An isolated unchanged form may not establish time.

solutions.AC9E3LA09-tricky-1: No. Looking away can indicate looking at another object, distraction or other possibilities; disagreement needs contextual evidence.
solutions.AC9E3LA09-tricky-2: No. Close framing makes detail prominent but readers may respond differently and gaze/context matters.
solutions.AC9E3LA09-tricky-3: Yes. A map can add location and route information; a diagram can show parts/relationships without a face.
solutions.AC9E3LA10-guided-1: The ribbon is 12 centimetres long and 5 millimetres wide. Accept equivalent accurate sentence with cm and mm if notation was taught; retain distinct units and dimensions.
solutions.AC9E3LA10-guided-2: Fen the mouse is a character. Setting: one rainy morning in a shed. Connected events include Fen finding a locked box, fetching a key and opening the box; any two clearly linked supplied events suffice.
solutions.AC9E3LA10-guided-3: The box is light means it weighs little; empty and enough to lift are clues. Lamp light means illumination that lets us see/read; lamp and read by support that meaning.
solutions.AC9E3LA10-guided-4: Rewrite: re- means again, so write again. Helpful: -ful makes an adjective meaning giving help/useful; the answer helped us. It does not mean any arbitrary base-plus-suffix combination is valid.
solutions.AC9E3LA10-tricky-1: No. Setting includes when as well as where.
solutions.AC9E3LA10-tricky-2: No. The resulting word and context determine meaning; -ly often makes an adverb describing how, but it is not one universal meaning or word-class rule (friendly is an adjective).
solutions.AC9E3LA10-tricky-3: No. Context supports the meaning intended in this sentence; it need not establish every dictionary sense or remove every ambiguity. Check another source when clues are insufficient.
